---
title: Importing a theme
description: Bring a shadcn, Zed, or VS Code theme into Atlas, and export one back out.
icon: Download
---

Atlas converts themes from three other formats. Open Settings with <Kbd>⌘,</Kbd>, choose **Appearance**, and click **Import**.

An import is a one-time conversion. What you get is an ordinary Atlas theme file in `~/.config/atlas/themes/`, which you then own and edit like any other. Nothing links back to the source, and Atlas never reads it again.

## How much each format carries

| Source | Verdict in the panel | Why |
|---|---|---|
| shadcn, tweakcn | **Nothing lost** | Atlas's base tokens *are* shadcn's tokens, so the chrome crosses verbatim |
| Zed | **Near-lossless** | Atlas's theme keys were modelled on Zed's roles |
| VS Code | **Lossy** | a workbench theme and an app theme are different things |

The format is detected from the content, so you paste and press **Convert** without saying which one it is.

## Give Atlas the theme

Three sources, as tabs at the top of the panel.

**Paste.** A shadcn registry item, a `globals.css`, a Zed theme family, or a VS Code colour theme, straight into the box.

**URL.** Fetched once over `http` or `https`, with a ten-second limit and a 4 MB cap. The file is converted and then forgotten.

**File.** Opens a picker for a `.json`, `.jsonc`, or `.css` file. This is the only source that can follow a VS Code `include`, because an `include` names a sibling file on disk.

Nothing is written until you press **Add theme**, so converting is free.

## shadcn and tweakcn

Two shapes are accepted, and they use the same mapping.

A **registry item**, which is what tweakcn exports and what a URL on a shadcn site serves:

```json
{
  "type": "registry:style",
  "cssVars": {
    "theme": { "radius": "8px", "font-mono": "\"JetBrains Mono\", monospace" },
    "light": { "background": "oklch(0.98 0.01 90)" },
    "dark": { "background": "oklch(0.18 0.02 280)" }
  }
}
```

Or a pasted **`globals.css`**, with `:root` and `.dark` blocks. `@theme inline` and `@layer base { :root { … } }` are read too.

**What crosses.** Every shadcn token name lands on the Atlas base token of the same name, per variant, with `cssVars.theme` or `@theme` sitting behind both. Values keep the notation you wrote them in, so an oklch theme stays oklch. The tweakcn extras land where Atlas has a home for them: `font-sans`, `font-serif`, `font-mono`, `radius`, `tracking-normal` (also read from `--letter-spacing`), and the composed `shadow-2xs` through `shadow-2xl` ramp.

**What is dropped.** The shadow ingredients (`--shadow-color`, `-opacity`, `-blur`, `-spread`, `-offset-x`, `-offset-y`), because Atlas takes the composed ramp rather than the recipe. Also a registry item's raw `css` block, and any CSS rule that is not `:root`, `.dark`, or `@theme`. An `@theme inline` entry of the form `--color-x: var(--x)` is a re-export rather than a value, and is skipped silently.

**What is kept but ignored.** `spacing`. Spacing and the type scale belong to the app, so the value stays in your file rather than being lost on a round trip, and the report warns that nothing honours it.

<Callout type="info">
  A shadcn token set describes application chrome and stops there. It has no vocabulary for an editor, a terminal, syntax, or a diff, so every one of those keys falls back to Atlas's own default for the appearance. Adding a [palette](/docs/themes/compatibility#what-a-shadcn-theme-cannot-say) is the step that fixes all of them at once.
</Callout>

**Which variant is which.** `cssVars.light` and `cssVars.dark` are trusted as written. In pasted CSS, `:root` is the light variant when there is a `.dark` block to be the other half. A dark-only paste is judged by the lightness of its `background` and filed as dark, and the report says so.

## Zed

A Zed theme file is a family, and each member becomes its own Atlas theme. Rosé Pine, Moon, and Dawn arrive as three siblings rather than as variants of one design, which is how the built-in themes already treat them.

**What crosses.** About 60 style keys map onto Atlas theme keys. All 16 `terminal.ansi.*` colours transfer exactly. `players[0].cursor` becomes `editor.caret` and `terminal.cursor`, and `players[0].selection` becomes the three selection keys. The `syntax` map collapses onto Atlas's 20 syntax roles, which is most of what near-lossless means for a code theme.

Zed's `border` becomes `border.default`, not `border`, because Atlas also has `border.variant` and a key may not be both a value and a prefix.

A scope that carries `font_style` is written as a styled key:

```toml
[dark.keys]
"syntax.comment" = { color = "#6e6a86", font_style = "italic" }
```

The style is preserved in the file. Atlas paints syntax from the colour.

**What is derived.** All 45 base tokens, because Zed has no shadcn layer to take them from. If the chrome looks off after an import, check `primary` (from `text.accent`), `accent` (from `element.hover`, since shadcn's `accent` is a hover surface), and `card` (from `elevated_surface.background`) first.

**What is dropped**, by category: icon roles, the `players[1..]` collaboration colours, editor furniture Atlas does not draw (wrap guides, invisibles, subheaders, the read and write highlight pair), app chrome that follows the panel tokens, the version-control states Atlas has no colour for (`conflict`, `renamed`, `ignored`, `hidden`, `unreachable`), `hint` and `predictive`, Zed's dim ANSI ramp, and whichever `syntax` scopes are finer than Atlas's 20 roles.

## VS Code

A converted VS Code theme is a starting point, not a copy. Expect to finish it by hand.

Around sixty of Atlas's theme keys have no workbench or TextMate equivalent at all, so a large part of the result is derived rather than stated. The panel shows you exactly which part before anything is written.

**Includes.** `include` is resolved relative to the file on disk, up to eight hops, with cycles caught. The included file is the base and the including file overrides it, and `tokenColors` are concatenated so that the includer's rules come last. A pasted theme cannot resolve an include, and the report names the file it could not read. The JSON-with-comments dialect that VS Code themes are actually written in is read as written.

**Appearance** comes from `type`. With no `type`, it is judged from the lightness of `editor.background`, and the report says that is what happened.

### Workbench keys

Mapped where Atlas has an equivalent: `editor.background`, `.foreground`, `.lineHighlightBackground`, `.selectionBackground`, `.foldBackground`, `editorCursor.foreground`, `editorGutter.background`, `editorLineNumber.*`, `editorBracketMatch.*`, `scrollbarSlider.*`, `editorWidget.background`, `sideBar.*`, `activityBar.background`, `input.background`, `tab.*`, `focusBorder`, `editorGroup.border`, `list.*`, `descriptionForeground`, `disabledForeground`, `input.placeholderForeground`, `textLink.foreground`, `editorError/Warning/Info.foreground`, `gitDecoration.added` and `deletedResourceForeground`, `diffEditor.inserted` and `removedText/LineBackground`, and all 16 `terminal.ansi*` plus `terminal.background`, `.foreground`, and `.selectionBackground`.

The base tokens are taken from `editor.background`, `foreground`, `editorWidget.background`, `dropdown.background`, `button.background` and `foreground`, `editorGroupHeader.tabsBackground`, `descriptionForeground`, `list.hoverBackground`, `list.activeSelectionForeground`, `editorError.foreground`, `editorGroup.border`, `input.border`, `focusBorder`, and `sideBar.*`.

Everything else is counted by category, each with the reason it had nowhere to go: editor furniture (minimap, rulers, indent guides, inlay hints, code lens, ghost text), widgets (suggest, hover, peek, notifications, quick input, menus, breadcrumbs, debug, testing), app chrome (status bar, title bar, badges, panel and sidebar headers, welcome page, settings, keybinding labels), version control (merge editor, the rest of `gitDecoration`, the source-control panel), icon roles, and terminal decorations.

### Why TextMate scopes cannot map perfectly

`tokenColors` is a list of rules carrying grammar *selectors*, not roles. A selector matches a scope when it is a dotted prefix of it, so `string` matches `string.quoted.double.ts`. VS Code then resolves a token by taking the longest matching selector, with a later rule winning a tie. A descendant selector such as `meta.tag entity.name` is a context rule, so only its rightmost element is considered.

That vocabulary describes a grammar, not a role. A theme is free to colour `string.quoted.double.ts` differently from `string.quoted.single.js`, and many do. Atlas has 20 syntax roles and no grammar inside the theme, so there is no rule that turns one into the other exactly.

The importer inverts VS Code's resolution instead. For each Atlas key it holds representative scopes and asks which rule VS Code would apply to each, first match winning:

| Atlas key | Scopes, in order |
|---|---|
| `syntax.comment` | `comment`, `comment.line`, `punctuation.definition.comment` |
| `syntax.keyword` | `keyword.control`, `keyword`, `storage.type`, `storage.modifier` |
| `syntax.operator` | `keyword.operator`, `keyword.operator.arithmetic` |
| `syntax.string` | `string.quoted.double`, `string` |
| `syntax.escape` | `constant.character.escape` |
| `syntax.regexp` | `string.regexp` |
| `syntax.number` | `constant.numeric` |
| `syntax.boolean` | `constant.language.boolean` |
| `syntax.null` | `constant.language.null`, `constant.language.undefined` |
| `syntax.constant` | `constant.other`, `constant.language`, `constant` |
| `syntax.type` | `entity.name.type`, `entity.name.class`, `support.type`, `storage.type.class` |
| `syntax.function` | `entity.name.function`, `support.function`, `meta.function-call` |
| `syntax.definition` | `entity.name.function.definition`, `entity.name`, `entity.name.namespace` |
| `syntax.variable` | `variable.other.readwrite`, `variable` |
| `syntax.property` | `variable.other.property`, `support.type.property-name`, `meta.object-literal.key` |
| `syntax.builtin` | `variable.language`, `support.class`, `support.constant` |
| `syntax.tag` | `entity.name.tag` |
| `syntax.attribute` | `entity.other.attribute-name` |
| `syntax.meta` | `meta.preprocessor`, `keyword.control.directive`, `entity.name.section` |
| `syntax.punctuation` | `punctuation.separator`, `punctuation` |

Use that table when a converted theme looks wrong in one place. A `syntax.type` that came out grey usually means the source theme said nothing about `entity.name.type` and everything about a grammar-specific scope below it.

`fontStyle: italic` on a matched rule survives as a styled key. `markup.*` and grammar-specific scopes have no Atlas role and are counted as dropped.

### Semantic tokens

`semanticTokenColors` takes precedence over `tokenColors`, because a theme that writes one is stating its intent more directly than a grammar selector can.

Only bare token types are read: `variable` and `parameter` become `syntax.variable`; `property` becomes `syntax.property`; `function` and `method` become `syntax.function`; `class`, `interface`, `struct`, `enum`, `type`, and `typeParameter` become `syntax.type`; `namespace` and `macro` become `syntax.meta`; `enumMember` becomes `syntax.constant`; and `keyword`, `comment`, `string`, `number`, `operator`, and `regexp` map onto their own keys.

A selector carrying modifiers, such as `variable.readonly.defaultLibrary`, is a conditional rule and cannot be applied unconditionally, so it is reported rather than used.

## Read the report

Every conversion produces a report, and the report is the point of the panel. Three counts sit at the top of each converted theme:

| Count | Means |
|---|---|
| **mapped** | the source said this, and Atlas kept it |
| **derived** | the source did not say it, so Atlas worked it out |
| **ignored** | the source said it and Atlas has nowhere to put it |

Beside them is the fidelity verdict, the variants the theme has, and a warning badge if committing would replace a theme you already imported or shadow a built-in.

Under the counts:

- **Summary lines** say what the format cannot carry. This is the part to read.
- **Warnings** are things that are wrong rather than merely absent: a `spacing` value Atlas will not honour, or an `include` that could not be resolved.
- **What was dropped** expands into one row per category, with a count and the reason. "22 workbench chrome" with "widgets and surfaces Atlas does not have" is an honest summary; a bare "ignored: 87" is not.
- **Mapped keys** and **Derived keys** expand into the full lists, each row a swatch, the fully qualified target such as `dark.base.background`, and where the value came from.

A high derived count is normal and not a problem. For a Zed theme it will be at least 45, because that is the whole shadcn layer. For a VS Code theme it will be much larger. What to look at is the derived list itself: those are the colours Atlas guessed, and they are the ones worth overriding by hand afterwards.

## Where the imported theme lands

Each converted theme gets a **Name** and an **Id** field. Edit them, then press **Add theme**.

Atlas writes `~/.config/atlas/themes/<id>.toml` and applies it immediately. The id is slugged first, so it always names a file inside that folder. The theme then appears in the picker marked **Local**, alongside the built-in ones.

From that point it is an ordinary theme file. See [authoring a theme](/docs/themes/authoring) for editing it, and the [token reference](/docs/themes/tokens) for what each key you might want to add controls.

<Callout type="warn">
  An id that matches a built-in theme replaces that built-in in the picker. The panel marks that case **Shadows a built-in** before you commit. Change the id unless overriding it is what you want.
</Callout>

## Export to shadcn

The same panel has an **Export** tab. Pick any theme, built-in or your own, and Atlas produces a shadcn `registry:style` item ready to copy:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://ui.shadcn.com/schema/registry-item.json",
  "name": "rose-pine",
  "type": "registry:style",
  "title": "Rosé Pine",
  "author": "Rosé Pine",
  "cssVars": {
    "theme": { "radius": "8px", "spacing": "0.25rem" },
    "dark": { "background": "#08070a", "foreground": "#e0def4" }
  }
}
```

The base tokens cross verbatim, one block per appearance, because shadcn's names are Atlas's names. `radius`, the three font stacks, `tracking-normal`, and `spacing` are appearance-independent, so they are hoisted into `cssVars.theme` and written once. A theme whose two variants disagree about the radius loses that disagreement, since shadcn cannot express it.

Everything above the base tokens is dropped: the palette, and every theme key covering the editor, terminal, syntax, diffs, team chat, and agent chips. shadcn has no vocabulary for any of them. The report gives the count and breaks it down by family, and notes when only one variant exists, since shadcn consumers usually expect both.

<Callout type="info">
  Exporting is for taking your colours to a shadcn project. To move a theme between two Atlas installs, copy the `.toml` instead. That loses nothing.
</Callout>
